body:
This is the exception.
People wish they were a fly on the wall.
I was in the room.
This is Kellyanne Conway. I was President Trump's Campaign Manager. I worked in the White House. I was there from the very beginning of MAGA. I can attest to the fact that the President has a finely tuned BS meter.
So I'm going to boil this text down to 3 important updates...
#1: I'm a pollster by trade - and the Generic Ballot has Democrats ahead by 4+ points.
#2: Republicans have one of the slimmest House Majorities in 100 years - and National Democrats just released their list of 35 vulnerable districts that will decide who wins the Midterms.
#3: We've lost 6 major elections in the last year, and we DO NOT have the resources to hold the line in the 35 targeted districts.
[Frankly, that last point could cost us the Midterms and open the door for another impeachment hoax against the President.](http://links.maga-conservatives.com/u/click?_t=da215d85003f407c964bf56cae76557f&_m=ee7752da1bd447f1b1255675289a25b6&_e=CUY1db_AWwFKvcEd4H_XJBri_HmN8XaYLFIrIDLsu7vac-9fjVTHrqfXED8K1cGR5llOBq-ELB4C-MAk8zYQ1l4BUlUe9Z0UuEceHmwEn-7U0xEMfCgv5RRJJ0M56XfltDYdQ_h0WpDSM2mvS4lJRGVk6HxL7Pa12riP5iewg-KY_sCPWMw0GDhM7ODXzu0wL1MXhB5eOITS28faNFxzEL2ceF2Klo7L_xlPK9wyqbnmr01nyHs9kHGAbiDjZKrg4Rl-u7vxz1qaQH6LjU4tYAdjz3zYeC7ZHi0k6DDRvxblYy8_3xuFTYhsrsh6gCMuc034QjzkTq3ySlX61B4IzDDS8FABXacBO-cQlV-ixuP8jK5l5tzf0rMN7IEpTLIaoSfqr7IdMMudCpc9sNPKzPzIHO5CSJFQfTYkEot0X5cQ9Fc70oZzjoFSO7apHwINMjTY0zCW2pVADDNHp9C2B8XZfTaLuFN4IYa754AzFyaWRfMVWZBSGVUq4JII6WYZtePGxCRIsVR2eZnGgZLyiU3TYZuMZO2gSXRcJzvkIwv7ODEV1eMKhhPndD1K3fFx_K0r3AWpMFuSsjKQ4AOk06USZNoTnZmrX-0Ic6tWyjIGWjQ0xE5tTvo__BtLiG0iACUk8i6WULs0OEbxsv0-1dkMDqq3xIfbVkKso121iBT9RG82vm_kYEaMPSEbPyoDr6BmDjlrNJBy2e63JQuKGl8khwQIrYeKABI2je_h408%3D)

[#Strongmaryland](https://dancoxforgovernor.us13.list-manage.com/track/click?u=866897dcd900340c866a1068a&id=76ef6027e1&e=5bb5efcda7) [#dancoxforgovernor](https://dancoxforgovernor.us13.list-manage.com/track/click?u=866897dcd900340c866a1068a&id=05035d2400&e=5bb5efcda7) [#nomoore](https://dancoxforgovernor.us13.list-manage.com/track/click?u=866897dcd900340c866a1068a&id=722bb12dfd&e=5bb5efcda7)

| Fellow Marylander,

It's bad. Wes Moore's administration responded, and it is shockingly dismal.

My MPIA (Maryland Public Information Act) Request came back with this information attached - with the Public Service Commission in charge of overseeing our utility rates providing ONE communication from the Governor's Office about our skyrocketing electric bills. ONE. And that was a January 15, 2026 Google Meeting (virtual) to tout his "legislative package" inviting his "Climate Partners" to participate. (See below).

This is worse than an insult. The lack of work and help by the Governor for Marylander's suffering peak electric and energy bills - the highest in the nation - is unconscionable.
* Where are the needed emergency executive actions?
* Where are the necessary numerous cabinet meetings?
* Where is Wes Moore's personal involvement in any meeting whatsoever?

Wes Moore is AWOL from fighting to lower ANY of your skyrocketing electric bills.
As I have said, Wes Moore is not working for you. He is focused on his national ambitions and wants to shiny-smile his way into national office.

I am a proven fighter for you. My wife and I care and that is why I am running for Governor. My running mate Rob Krop cares as well, and together we will lower your costs and make Maryland affordable.

As your Governor, I will immediately:
* lower our energy costs and stabilize our electric grid by rebuilding and/or bringing all 14 Democrat-closed power plants back online by emergency order,
* provide emergency assistance to the most vulnerable and ensure we receive immediate relief from and removal of the hidden RGGI and EmPower taxes of 30% in our bills,
* expand our LNG power plants and distribution, and
* fast-track the review and work of Maryland with the federal authorities to safely bring onto the grid Small Modular Reactors which are the future of inexpensive, clean and stabilizing energy.

Wes Moore is leaving Maryland behind. I am asking for your immediate [support ](https://dancoxforgovernor.us13.list-manage.com/track/click?u=866897dcd900340c866a1068a&id=e6cbe2dacb&e=5bb5efcda7)of any amount to take him on now to win. With your help, together we will win.

[](https://dancoxforgovernor.us13.list-manage.com/track/click?u=866897dcd900340c866a1068a&id=1cf66d77f0&e=5bb5efcda7)

Thank you for standing together with us.

For Freedom,

Dan Cox
DanCoxforGovernor.com
Renew Maryland!

But behind the music, the laughter and the packed hotels, there is another race happening. A darker one. Because when hundreds of thousands of visitors arrive, traffickers arrive too. They move quietly.
They hide in plain sight.
And vulnerable children can become targets. Human trafficking is now one of the fastest-growing crimes in our nation. And events like this create the perfect cover. Busy hotels. Constant movement. Strangers everywhere. That's why, _before the first horse ever leaves the gate_, we're taking action.

**A whisper of hope.** These kits are delivered to hotels and motels across the city. **Placed quietly. The Sound of Freedom Foundation is a faith-driven movement on a mission to **_stop the sale of God 's children_. ** We support the front lines. clean_body: Before the big race, we're preparing to protect vulnerable children across Louisville. | | | | | | GOD'S CHILDREN ARE NOT FOR SALE | | | Peter,Soon Louisville will come alive. Bright floral hats. Mint juleps in hand. Crowds dressed in their finest. And the thunder of hooves racing toward the finish line. It 's a time of celebration. A tradition. A moment people wait all year for. But behind the music, the laughter and the packed hotels, there is another race happening. A darker one. Because when hundreds of thousands of visitors arrive, traffickers arrive too. They move quietly. They hide in plain sight. And vulnerable children can become targets. Human trafficking is now one of the fastest-growing crimes in our nation. And events like this create the perfect cover. Busy hotels. Constant movement. Strangers everywhere. That's why, before the first horse ever leaves the gate, we're taking action. Across Louisville, volunteers are stepping forward. Ordinary people, just like you. They are being trained to spot the warning signs of trafficking and to understand what is happening right in their own city. To refuse to look away. Then, together, they prepare simple but powerful tools. Soap. Makeup remover wipes. Each one labeled with the national human trafficking hotline. A lifeline. A whisper of hope. These kits are delivered to hotels and motels across the city. Placed quietly. But with great purpose. Because sometimes, a child sees that number and realizes escape is possible. The Sound of Freedom Foundation is a faith-driven movement on a mission to stop the sale of God 's children. We support the front lines. We work closely to prevent trafficking, equip rescue efforts, and train everyday people to recognize the signs, so children can be protected before exploitation happens. The Sound of Freedom Foundation exists for this reason. To stop the sale of God 's children. After producing Sound of Freedom , I knew awareness was not enough. Real children still needed protection. So this mission continues through real action: Preventing exploitation. Supporting rescue efforts. Equipping communities. And bringing light into the darkest places. Jesus said, "Whoever welcomes one little child like this in my name welcomes me. " (Matthew 18:5) As the city prepares for celebration, we must prepare for protection. Because once the crowds arrive, the window to act begins to close. This is our moment. Before the race, the crowds and before traffickers fully move in. Will you help us with a donation of $25, $60, $120 or whatever you're able to do today to help reach more hotels, equip more volunteers, and reach more children who may be waiting for hope? Your gift today can help: $60 -- Equip one outreach visit $120 -- Supply life-saving materials $180 -- Expand outreach across multiple hotels $240 -- Multiply protection before peak crowds arrive Imagine, amid the cheers, the celebration, the roses and the race, a child finds a way out. Because someone like you chose to act. Please give as generously as you can today and please pray for every volunteer walking into those hotels and for every child who needs rescue. Because God 's children are not for sale. And together, we will run this race to protect them. With gratitude and prayer, Eduardo Verastegui Sound of Freedom, Producer For the Sound of Freedom Foundation 6671 Southwest Freeway, Suite 700, Houston TX 77074 |

subject: Whether by his Cabinet or Congress, the President must be removed from office.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for Congress
body:
We are playing with the brink.
#
Trump's [statement tonight](https://act.ocasiocortez.com/go/36437?t=1&akid=11142%2E2526796%2EhVziUX) changes nothing.
The President has threatened a genocide against the Iranian people, and is continuing to leverage that threat.
He has launched a massive war of enormous risk and of catastrophic consequence without reason, rationale, nor Congressional authorization — which is as clear a violation of the Constitution as any. Each day this goes on, the risk and criminality of these actions escalate for our nation and the world.
Moreover, this administration’s self enrichment, insider trading, and pure corruption off this chaos — from crypto currencies to predictive trading markets to bribe “settlements” — has placed the Trump administration’s pursuit of personal wealth squarely against the wellbeing of our nation and its people.
All of these incidents, and plenty more, have clearly driven our country past the threshold for impeachment or invocation of the 25th amendment.
We cannot risk the world nor the wellbeing of our nation any longer. None of these considerations should be partisan, but shared in good faith by Americans of all backgrounds who care for the safety and stability of the United States.
Whether by his Cabinet or Congress, the President must be removed from office. We are playing with the brink.
More soon,
Alexandria

name: Tom Leonard
subject: April 7th - Positive Path Newsletter
body:
[](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/qFVB41bL2G06QurSg81h2w/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw)
---
Dear Friend,

April's starting off strong! I hope you all had a wonderful and relaxing Easter weekend.

This past week on the campaign trail was great. We're continuing to build our coalition, and meet more local community leaders throughout the state.

Here are some highlights:
1. On Wednesday, I toured GARR Tool in Alma, spending time talking with local leaders in that community and sharing our policy plans that will help Michigan manufacturing.
2. On Thursday, I was interviewed by Bill Spadea on New Jersey's #1 radio show, talking about the madness of data centers and how they're not only affecting our home state.
3. On Friday, Jenell and I went to the Tigers opening day game, having a chance to talk with the people of Detroit and enjoy the day while also spreading our plan for a better Michigan.
4. And on this past Monday, our team attended a data center meeting in South Lyon, continuing our mission to bring The Path Forward to local communities, and stop this AI data center madness.

---
Together, we are creating The Path Forward.
**Empowering Michigan 's Workers and Businesses**
Michigan's work force is essential to our state, and it's disgusting what burdens have been placed on them and business leaders throughout the last few years.

_Here 's the problem:_

Michigan's occupational licensing system imposes unnecessary burdens on workers, with requirements that often lack practical justification. Since the repeal of Right to Work in March 2024, Michigan's unemployment rate has increased from 3.9% to 5.5%, making our state the second-worst in the nation for employment.

Meanwhile, the Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC) continues to spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually on corporate welfare programs that pick economic winners and losers--initiatives that have consistently failed to produce results.

_Here 's my solution:_

As Governor, I will adopt universal license reciprocity and make Michigan the easiest state in the country in which to work. If you are certified in another state, you will be able to work here immediately: no bureaucratic hoops or delays.

I will restore Right to Work to empower Michigan's workers. No one should be forced to join a union as a condition of employment. Right to Work laws protect worker freedom and drive economic growth. In fact, nine of the ten fastest-growing states in 2023 were Right to Work states.

By prioritizing service over special favors, we will create a truly business- friendly environment that promotes innovation, opport unity, and prosperity for all Michigan businesses and workers.
**Join the Team!**
It's with your help that results come. We would love to have you join the team!

• Volunteer Today: Sign up for phone banking, door-knocking, events, or hosting a meet-and-greet in your community. Your time makes all the difference! [Sign Up Here](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/j1PwjePHOc7892jc1iXZLBXg/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw) and reach out to our Field Director, Tony, for more volunteer opportunities at [tony@tomformichigan.com](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/FC2R1p892LdR4wZcmhm3XKnw/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw)

• Continue sharing our positive vision on social media - follow my X account's, [@Tom4Michigan](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/vOh9weQe6pLEjSUnxMJFzg/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw) and [@TomLeonard28](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/JU2mAwuOKX6ykBXwQToTzg/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw), my [Facebook page](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/88NwBx4J0Xf2KSJtyDfHqw/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw), my [Instagram](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/VxfJGfFlZ8qTL1OvzwhXDg/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw), and my [TikTok](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/ztpz37PhdAE1E892yU763763jogw/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw).
---
Thank you for your continued support of our vision, and helping us share our Path Forward for Michigan across the state. Let's keep our momentum going into this upcoming week, and throughout the rest of April!
---

God bless you and your loved ones. Have a great week.

Best,

**Tom Leonard**
Candidate for Governor
To learn more, get involved, and donate visit [www.TomForMichigan.com](https://sendy.right-strategies.us/l/cve9YluPeAoOO3uAO6KV4g/YjSryVU5EPwlDrHSX892AGEA/zZtJZNVkmt7pahJWqIuTzw)

name: Judge Chris Taylor
subject: We won!
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Chris Taylor for Justice
body:
I’m deeply honored and grateful to share that we’ve won our race for the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
#
Friends,
I’m deeply honored and grateful to share that we’ve won our race for the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
This victory belongs to all of us. To everyone who showed up, spoke out, and believed in what we could build together — **thank you**.
Over the course of this campaign, I had the privilege of meeting so many Wisconsinites. I heard your stories, your hopes, and your belief that our justice system should work for everyone.
That’s what carried us across the finish line.
I’ve spent my career as a lifelong advocate for fairness and protecting the rights of all people, and I remain committed to ensuring everyone who comes before the court is heard, respected, and treated equally.
**It is the honor of a lifetime to continue this work on the Wisconsin Supreme Court.**
Thank you again for being part of this. We couldn’t have done it without you.
With gratitude,
Judge Chris Taylor

| | [READ IN APP](https://open.substack.com/pub/melissa4congress/p/freedom-cannot-depend-on-last-minute?utm_source=email&redirect=app-store&utm_campaign=email-read-in-app)
---

In frightened times, people start asking a certain kind of question.
_**Who will stop this?**_
Will the courts step in? Will some principled official refuse the order? Will a general draw a line? Will there be some last-minute act of courage from somewhere above ordinary life?
I understand the instinct. Fear looks for a strong hand. Chaos looks for a final guardrail. When people feel the ground shifting under their feet, they start scanning the horizon for a rescuer.
But that is the wrong place to put our hope.
**Freedom cannot depend on last-minute heroes.**
A free country is not supposed to function like a disaster movie, with the public waiting breathlessly for one decent person inside a powerful institution to save the day in the final scene. A constitutional republic is supposed to be built so lawless power hits barriers early and often. Rights. Hearings. Courts. Oversight. Accountability. An independent press. Organized communities. A public that refuses to be intimidated. That is how freedom is supposed to work.
That is what due process is _for_.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/bfb2da94-b84d-4aa3-b3a8-8a6a2003e31a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
And that is why due process is **not a technicality.**
It is not legal decoration. It is not red tape. It is not a loophole for bad people. It is one of the core structures that keeps fear from becoming a system of government.
Due process means the state does not get to simply point at a person and say: "they're a bad guy, trust us."
It means _**notice**_. It means a hearing. It means a chance to answer an accusation. It means an opportunity to challenge evidence. It means neutral review. It means rules that bind officials too, not just the people underneath them.
That is not weakness. That is _civilization_.
The people who sneer at due process usually do so in the language of urgency. They tell you the threat is too serious, the danger too immediate, the stakes too high. They imply that process is for quieter times. They want you to believe fairness is a luxury we can no longer afford.
But that is exactly backward.
Due process matters most when fear is highest.
Rights that evaporate the moment the public is scared are not rights. A Constitution that only functions when everyone is calm is not much of a Constitution. If due process does not hold for the unpopular, the vulnerable, the foreign-born, the accused, the politically inconvenient, or the easy-to-scapegoat, then it does not truly hold for anyone.
This is one of the oldest tests in civic life: do our principles still apply when fear enters the room?
If the answer is no, then what governs us is not law.
**It is panic, power, and mood.**
And mood is a terrible foundation for a country.
One of the most dangerous things about authoritarian drift is not only what the strongman does. It is what everyone else begins to assume they must wait for. A judge. A general. A prosecutor with a conscience. A heroic insider. Some decency from above, arriving just in time.
But that is already a sign of democratic erosion.
In a healthy republic, ordinary people should not have to pray for elite defection in order to preserve liberty. The protection is supposed to be built into the architecture itself. That is what constitutional order means. It means no one is supposed to become so powerful, or so unrestrained, that the public must pin its hopes on a last-minute act of personal heroism.
Heroism matters. Moral courage matters. I will never say otherwise.
But **freedom that depends on extraordinary courage at the top, rather than ordinary accountability throughout the system, is already in danger.**
And that danger becomes most visible when government starts governing through intimidation.
A constitutional government does not rule by intimidation.
A free society does not require fear to function.
When agencies become known less for fairness than for terror; when people start wondering whether showing up for a hearing is safe; when rights exist on paper but not in lived reality; when official power begins to feel arbitrary, selective, and untouchable -- we are not looking at "tough governance." **We are looking at a breach in the basic promise of the republic.**
My own family knows that personally.
My husband, a disabled American veteran, was wrongfully detained by federal immigration authorities. We fought in federal court and brought him home. That experience did not make me contemptuous of law. It made me more committed to it. Because when process collapses, families pay the price. When institutions stop honoring their own constraints, the human cost is immediate. It lands in kitchens and courtrooms and children's lives. It lands in the body.
This is why I reject the lazy framing that due process is some kind of indulgence.
No. Due process is what stands between a free people and a government that can simply decide who counts, who waits, who vanishes into paperwork, and who gets heard only after the damage is done.
It is one of the ways the law proves it still binds the powerful.
And that matters not only in immigration, but everywhere.
If the state can bypass fair procedure for one group because they are unpopular, one day it will find a reason to bypass it for another. If hearings become optional when the target is easy to caricature, the category of people unworthy of full rights will keep expanding. It always does. History is grimly consistent on this point. Power rarely stays neatly confined to the people it first reaches for.
That is why the answer cannot be to wait for rescue.
The answer has to be stronger and more democratic than that.
We need courts willing to enforce the Constitution, yes.
We need journalists willing to investigate abuse, yes.
We need public servants with integrity, yes.
We need people inside institutions to remember their oath, yes.
But above all, **we need a public culture that understands what those institutions are for.** We need communities that do not accept the disappearance of their neighbors into silence. We need civic organizations, faith communities, local leaders, lawyers, watchdogs, and ordinary people who know that self-government is not spectator sport.
_**The people are not the audience of freedom. They are its keepers.**_
That means elections still matter.
It means local democratic life matters.
It means oversight matters.
It means refusing propaganda matters.
It means telling the truth in plain language matters.
It means building systems sturdy enough that no family has to wonder whether the law will suddenly stop protecting them because somebody in power decided expedience mattered more than principle.
And it means growing up, politically, past the fantasy that someone else will always save us.
This is one of the hardest lessons of citizenship: **the republic is not self-sustaining.** It requires maintenance. It requires memory. It requires courage that is not glamorous. It requires the willingness to show up before the emergency, not just to pray for a savior during it.
That is why due process belongs at the center of our politics.
Not because we are soft.
Because we are serious.
Serious about liberty. Serious about equal protection. Serious about public safety that does not become state abuse. Serious about a country where rights mean something in practice, not just in speeches.
The stronger our due process protections, the less we have to gamble on heroics.
The stronger our accountability systems, the less room there is for intimidation to become normal.
The stronger our civic culture, the less likely we are to mistake raw power for order.
That is the work before us.
Not rescue fantasies. Not passive dread. Not waiting for someone above ordinary life to remember their conscience and throw the switch in time.
We need something sturdier than that.
We need a country where freedom does not depend on last-minute heroes because the guardrails are real, the law still binds, the people still care, and the Constitution still means what it says.
That is not a small demand.
But it is the minimum.
And finishing that work is still up to us.

## Trump Pauses Iran Strike Deadline
President Trump said Tuesday he would [delay planned military escalation against Iran](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGunDAQRb_GdLMygxfYwkUaupc2JTJ4_JjE2MgeHtp8fUSK_ECaKeZKRzrnx8f84Thy-vzudrIS8pzoqpFEqMxcXFrJVQpcyBWhnSvzseUZNfagDehx9o7jezaNt4EIqWvItsPw7A2Or77ZrO6HJ61-XEa9Gt-6JbTY9QMOiM_eub5he9O00WOr9dg-H2Gk7mXGpaXFvzqnldHkWXJ5_MycZKMQ3_mLymPNexPtJnJU1X1TOCmc0vvIVe5J4XSDFU7a3GdQOF25RA-3osJJyrkf4FLKZ1qpglwZLqJf4PO5RILKnjz8CwBbPkuFhUIuBHcb8OR85ESwcZIKsjm5fxG4whpzJZAMgZOL_Ju8wqkp1h8Xx8i1H5TRn7vj-NdD_iv-l8U_AQAA___00Zr4) for two weeks, less than 90 minutes before his 8 p.m. deadline, if Tehran agrees to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump said the pause followed talks with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir, and described the proposal as a "[double-sided ceasefire](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFutDAQhJ_GdEa2WcBXuPgbuvvblMic18dGC0bGB7k8fUReIeVopBl938d9vHtiWp___YKuxDSueO6MpWAeKfv1gX7HSBl9LrjQTrTNaTTKdFKBVHYMnvg9QhVcRDTYVOh037cdGHvrqtlBiBqCavveG20fjY4tTAChCRqmqYsVuWtNgbJaKavbOlpsbmAnjVO4NV4JUBiopFx_JlrLjJHf6cBcP9JSsZtL2XbR_BNmEGY4z7OO6euiuHphBqYD5ZWFGUp-LZu8uGRAH5hWlLRnjyznlJfXt_RbJpZ9lV3YTmKmvesFqOfiiX8Py58sHc78BAAA___kmX2D)" tied to a broader peace framework. The announcement came after a day of sharp escalation, including [Trump's earlier threat](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0L1u8yAUxvGrgS3R4cMYDwyv9MpbOlXqaBE4xKfCxgKSKHdfpbfQ9Xmk3_D_uiwXT5n224ff0PVUlh2fLWPvWBeqfg_oGyaq6GvHjRrRsZZFgjQn0CewS_SUX4vm0SVEiYqjE-M4GC3tZPjqlAlplDEYa2VUQ0JrYPBDHCFoUCFwcm8NNFgBYMVwThbVpO1V4DVOygPTgJF6qefvQntfMeVXeWA9h7Lx7Nbej8bUPyZnJude731tJZDP7_89aqjo8_-y-xw_6307mJyP0npjchbCKKOUMqDUNA2TEby6eDwpZ2pmZBpum6dfivc_9Xk4-RMAAP__dZB3jQ) that "a whole civilization" could die if Iran did not make a deal, along with reports of fresh U.S. strikes on Iran's oil hub at Kharg Island and Israeli attacks on bridges and rail lines. Iran's Supreme National Security Council later said it had accepted a two-week ceasefire, and Trump said Tehran had proposed a "workable" 10-point peace plan.
## Medicare Advantage Funding Jumps 2.48%
The Trump administration finalized a [2.48% payment increase](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkb2unDAQhZ_GdF55jS82hYuNruhumhQp0SweYLL-QbZZxNtH3DxCqpG-GY10vvP7a_wC8hSXnxDQ1jmNEY_isVbMI2WIE0LBmTJCrhioEG1rGqWQHReKCzM6IH-OqnF2RpTYNmjvWn90Spq-a1arTWeMA62ePU5mVsopB8IpPfVa9GAastc3oYS5C2HuH7fZYNsr87zj0_UtCKYEOqop3_4kinXF2Z_pjfk2pdB4u9a6FdY-mByYHI7juIUSrx2TA0a-FyaHkCKe14T8wnqRvfCaeAYqyAM6miAjB_eGWGFBvsEZMNbvI4plz5gLf55cKsMpcimk_scvQ7zUNL0KL3tekMkBMn88pKCX-GTtkCZyrP38cUnGo_zCvDXZuu0g76l0mimxBCD_Haf-VwdvK_8GAAD__-7bnP8) for Medicare Advantage plans in 2027, a significantly higher increase than originally proposed, totaling more than $13 billion in additional federal funding for private insurers. The rate is a reversal from the [0.09% increase proposed in January](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkMHKnTAQhZ8m7pRJMpq4yKJQ3P3ddimJGa_TJioxvXLfvthX6OZw4MDH4fv5NX95Try_fvhMrq7HvNN9JaqVyszF7wv5i1Yu5EulzBfzuR2zAjW0gC3YOXpOnxmb6FYiRbohJ43pB1R2HJrNWTSaDOoYEdXovYwocbEaxz7EANiwe2iAYCWAlX23WtIj2iApxFF7EAgUuR6l-3XwXjda0-d4U-mWIzfJbbWel9DfhJqEmu777pY9LM8o1PSghZoAn3haLX_y2WaKvPhCrY9vv1f_om6rOQk95etYfnMU-rsEXJUZTUAZBwMKQi81jjL0AYah901x8bw5Jb4GIxBe2XP696n-l8i3U38DAAD__7NtgpM), which had threatened to force insurers to slash benefits or hike premiums for the 35 million seniors enrolled in the plans. Shares of major insurers soared in after-hours trading, with Humana jumping roughly 12% while UnitedHealth rose more than 9%. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said the update ensures coverage remains affordable and that patients "get real value" from their plans as medical and insurance costs continue to rise.
## Artemis II Sends Photos from the Dark Side
The Artemis II crew completed a [historic flyby of the moon Monday](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGOhCAQBuCnwQ6DyCIUFNfY7bVXmlHGdS4IGyB6-_YXN_cGV04m-f98_9d9ugMFio9P2NHVNU0RzxKwVswTZYgLQsGVMkKuuFMhem5pkkJqLhQXZvJA4TWpxrsVUWLfoOuG4aaVNFY3m1tmowdY1Ow9Lkr6TqP1Vt5mDcJYsA25K00oYTohTHdrV4O9VWbucPa2B8GUQE815fY7UawbruGVDsztkvYmuK3WZ2H9B5Mjk-N5nu2afi7F9WdyDHQgv24mxz8EJ-IRCvA9pch3KoVSfHsGLnWTnX-eFAIVPTAlHjtQeJfVfy10OPkbAAD__wC6eyE), becoming the first humans to circle it in more than 50 years, and now heads back to Earth for a splashdown Friday evening. As the spacecraft passed behind the moon, the astronauts lost contact with Earth for about 40 minutes, flying in complete radio silence on the far side before signals were restored. [Follow the crew live here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykj71uwyAURp8GtliXn2AyMHTJlq4dEZhLfCtsLECJ8vZVqr5B50_f0TlfN38LVGi_f4YN3cjV7_jsBcfA5qmFfcHQMVPD0AZu1ImOtXoJ0pxAn8D6FKi8vObJZUSJiqMT83w2WtqL4avLygDM7wNGkU2KIKRQdtHnqFAI5OTeI2iwAsCK85Qtqou2UWBMFxWAacBEo7bpu9I-VszlVR_YpqVuvLh1jKMz9cHklcnrn2YKfY01tDT1IyzI5JU3l44nlULdzEzDfQtUfhHjX90PJ38CAAD__05ybA8). The crew captured a stunning "Earthset" image as Earth slipped below the lunar horizon and witnessed a nearly hour-long solar eclipse from deep space. [See the image here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkb2unDAQhZ_GdCBj81tQoCRIt9hUkVKiWTNcJjI2sr1LtsmzRxj2CW4z5xsOPvbYv2_jDUiT-fwJK3ZhtqPB3WsMAd1IDoxC8DiTQ3ABV_JE22JHwUWV8iLlzTgB6ddYJFM3IwqUCXZ5XZdVIZq2SpYuz1toZq5yWYK6Kw5CIlZ1q0A0HKFMqDvSeMGbnPMmL7O5QdkWzT3H-9RK4KzgOFGwLvtjyYQFZ_2yT3SZsmuiuyWEzTPZMzEwMez7nilzV4fJxHBEMzHw4ig1E8M1RkqUrtaaFJWmzWPqHyY14CFbwqqZkEz2_5jsA_4NTH7_tSATpeD9uTryx0cU5XA_AbbwcDjFJizXX0-6bDtHARPlB7iweAyndX7rN0c6UnXUbxHPAd4d-CsdXxFmfaWDsw_z3vo8681akyWum7adtCZf1azgnyuQjhcXvvTaz078DwAA__96B7H1). In a tearful moment, the astronauts named an unnamed crater after Commander [Reid Wiseman's late wife, Carroll](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkD2OpTAQhE8DWSNjDA8CB5uQzaYboga3H73yD7J7hp3br2b0bjBZqUoqVX1_3rY35MDp-RsjWfF5S3TXQCJUNi6YDsJKngthEYpcma8zb1rpCZQBNW8OOXxupnXWE2kaWrL94zFORs_L1J72MJPeDal-0pMenBqNGYcFl9Ht0-xRtWy_2pRRc6_U3I-dn2lYzLz3tLtlQNUYRY4ll-5v5iQn-fCZP6h0R45tsKfIVZvhV6PXRq_3fXf1woO-0kav3xro3xVyQeGcGr2-rjR6jTkniBRzYQzw8kEDVik54btUSBgJwnvCAnvh5ylQryyAXqhA5Fo5JzhyjJgclQoBheBmT22x7ro5BK7TozHqGZHD92b5EegPq_8HAAD__wgulq8), who died of cancer in 2020, calling it a "bright spot" visible from Earth. Early photos reveal the 600-mile-wide Orientale basin, ancient lava flows, and craters never before seen by human eyes. [See the photos here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOtSAUhJ9GOwwiIhYUf2N3_3ZLc4TD9WwQDJBr7ttvvNk32GommWQm33w91gdQoPj8Dwea6tMa8SoBa8W8UoZoEQp6ygi54kGF6NzTKrhQjEvG9eqAwnuVrTMeUeDQoumnaVRS6Fm1uxm00MNsPYx6s2rWbtpgG3vl515rFK4lc7dxyXXPue7HzmscZqm3Hjc3D8AbydFRTbn7ThTrjj680wtzZ9PRBrPXepZm-NeIpRHLdV1d3OxNceeNWIoljBZvd8JHzz3VVFiEAuwXixGxI6XIso0glBoVb7Nx50UhUFFTI_nzAAqfzfqno15G_AQAAP__7bh9Ww).

## Paxton Investigating Solar Companies
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has [launched an investigation](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDGOrSAUQFejHQYQFQuK39i9305pGLkoyRUMXPW5-8m8LcwCzsnJ-XrNLxswxPW_3cHQ26c5wl0QiCDPoe3KmS94lrQfCASr3aFsJ82Sy55xxbienQ34zKp25pu7UdRgxDB0veqFEPVmhq6X4Dvp1AjtCGqEvtXK21EOPSyDroP5lXHFtRBcKN043WnlBw--1V07jpXi4AKl3NAGBG9bPD7pgtwsaa_RbERHqdp_lZwqOd333RwXI1i2JuW1ktMHYZYo5QgPWyFCtshCvKBQWC1BYRlKcBApWGQloc0sxEIWEXJhPmXmsz3diRCJHdkuFBYolZzqbNxxB8RQ-qFSfN1twE8X_e3mZeRPAAAA__9Y241V) into four residential solar power companies for alleged violations of the state's Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act. In a press release, Paxton claimed his office had received more than 100 formal complaints against San Antonio-based CAM Solar Inc., Houston-based Lone Star Solar Services LLC, San Francisco-based SunRun Inc., and Freedom Forever LLC of Temecula, California. "_Thousands of Texans have been targeted by companies selling solar panel systems, and it's imperative that these companies are held responsible for any lies or deceptive marketing they use_ ," [Paxton said](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDGunTAQRVcDnZHNM2AKF2noftqUaLAHcGJsZA_w2H3EU7KC341GR1f3nl9f4xc478LyEzbU9J7jGPDKHokwje7V5COdeJu47R4JF9gwrweNNa9bxiXjarTg_D3K0uqJ216UqEXXNa1shRDlqhtrVW9a209CtQbmCWwvUPLeNApMK0unnzAuuRKCC6kqqxol527G-aWaV98XkqN1FFNFKxK-Ic_-jiemysSt9Hol2nPx-lHUQ1EP13VVHwiIYgp4Lxgwga-WeBb18Kwr6iGhR8j4nP859g9kfzCwHd4UA_NwBLNiZhv8jom54MgBuROZidsExC5nMe8JwbI5wWGf_w7BYWYZ_SO2TNrul_Pe5bYrJF82cP7TnL7n-9T13wAAAP__gNabYA). Consumer group Texas Appleseed has [collected statements](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOhCAYhJ9GOw0gCFtQXGO3115pWPlZSX4WA__q-vYX7xWum2QmM5nv5z7fXcT4en67BJY-Ic8vOCoCEZQ5Dqq-yw7nktOGQPB0Cer6plkwMXZMdszM3kU8Z9l6-2D-xluwXGs1ypFz3q7WKKENLEYZCcIH7fTwUFpLJvkIyos22quMSWY4Z1ya3l_ZoAOEwajhdmskAx8pl55WIPi4GvDMO5R-yalFuxJttRm-GjE1YjqOoz_dmvPlNmK67jRicoXignDJPS4UU-08LLBR3KGrGV3pqkOoHUKgjkvF5Kgl61dK2BbrtyMixjrqRrJnchH_xul_yHYrfgMAAP__LAl_-A) from multiple alleged victims of fraudulent solar power companies, and Houston outlets ABC13 and KPRC 2 have interviewed customers of [Freedom Forever](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLGSgyAURb8GOzKAqFhQbGOXbbd0XsJDmUVw4MXEv99JfmHrO_fOPefnOl8hxJCWb9jQ0svnOeGzRiTCMoe2q49y4HnP2x6RcIEN6_qgWQnVc6G5MLODEM9ZN87ehBtlg1YOQ9frXkrZrNYohEFIpU03en0bW2NaFL43vfceZdcE-x4TWhgphdTm4kxntB88-tZ07TgyLdAFyuVCKxK-oPp45gPL5Z63JtqVaK-s_WJqYmqC212274Spac-VmJo-HQ5EuSQ8-YIJC0T-i4nv8KKceEgHVgoLEFZec4TCd0gY-RscUsDKfVhW4r7AwzE1SWO0GUfF1NQU6_ZniDHUfmBaLBuE-LlG_xN6WPUXAAD__0GQixI) and [SunRun](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2ypCAQhZ8GM6YA8WcCgk3M7qYbWj3QaNeiWNKjd95-i32Fm3TUdb7znT9f8xdQon35DRs6_o553vEuCZnxnKntyvu88OPzdiRkXGDDsr55Nsr0UlmpxjkApc9sm-BeKjx1g04PQ9fbXmvdrE7H9mmGFlS0r-j7l1IjqNBh71XwXXw15GqYsmrUWmk7PsLYjTYOEWM7du3zKazCQJzPB6_I-A0lpk--8Hz4vDXJrcxHEe0vYSZhpvu-Hz6R_2vW_C6c9_olzFS1hJlS9pCEmSpTmEnZelphpsLAKGm_sDAtwFhkyQlOWd1hJyyyMqVPQFuROcqAHg-mC2WBi_alSJ93PsFzBTWnC8dNKVHpB2HVsgGl_435ZztfzvwLAAD__23_k-A) who claimed they were charged more than $130,000 for agreements they were pressured to sign and didn't fully understand.
## TxDOT Asks for Input on I-35
TxDOT is [seeking public input](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykUL2upCAYfRrsMIAIWlBsYzfbbmkY-VAyKAY-dXz7jfcVbnNykpOcv3-_9-xpxP8AAAD__519jZ8) on the future of I-35 to "identify existing gaps and evolving multimodal transportation needs and opportunities" over the next 25 years. Known as the Main Street of Texas, I-35 stretches approximately 590 miles from Laredo to the Texas-Oklahoma border and serves a region that's home to about half of the state's population. Click [here](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2SrCAUhJ8GMyz-VAwIbmI2N93QwuEg1OJgwVFn3n5rZh9h467u6u_7us03G1N8rP_tBgafPs8PuGoCRChzlF09ygmve972BAir3aCGA2fBRE-ZokzPzsb0mlXjzMLcyBswfBi6XvWc8yYYC3dv5aCV6oX2ehFOSGntopnybhRjE817jCmmOWdc6dbpTis_ePBSd3IciWLgIubSYgCEp60-vfIJpb3nrUkmIO6VyH9ETERM13W1-HQZ2zWfREx2yQcSMb2xSs4bEVNFi3BFB0RMaL-BYoiVfkr0l5dipgHSTmuw-zsH6g88CtDsaZRdG3BLTTFuv2JKsfYDUWzdbEyfT_g3k6cRPwEAAP__sbWKgw) to complete the survey, which is available until May 6. "_I-35 is one of the most important interstates for the state of Texas and our nation, supporting Texas' economy and quality of life_ ," [said](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLHOozAQhJ_GdI68xgZTuLiG7r_2SmTs3cSKwQg2kLz9KfcKV89oNN_352f6Cbnk9f47LOj5TXVa8ToKMuM-5dYer_3ET6zLVpDxHhY8Hi-etNKdVEYqN6WQy2cyTfKzSgM06KHvbWc6AGgefiaiuR-6VsHc4qCAAqYEdiZysQvUZP8dU0Y5AAXG3ZKzzlBPSK2z7TAIozBlrvuNH8j4DgeVTz1xv8W6NMU_mLdDtL-EHoUer-u6PSOufH5jocewc44FhR6_ZEKPpcZQhB75nSrLcDzzepd53V4ss2ytzMu21xMXXPlbt0rJuUspEoFEACPNEEAOEKwM0JKKvdPYU7P7tF25lHx0vTDqvoRc_l3k_xN7ev03AAD__7X3i_A) TxDOT Transportation Planning and Programs Director Humberto "Tito" Gonzalez Jr. The [comprehensive study](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLtuhDAURL_GdCC_MYWLNHSbNiVy8DU4Mmtk34Xl76PdKn260Wh0NDpft-nmYor35dNtYPEZ8nSHsyZAhDJFoeqjHHDNedsTICxug7o-cOKU65bKlprJu5iuSTbeflM_sAYs63ulpWaMNavtZypAKQNBSNV7KYQOlDs5DEzMQesm2heMSmoYo0yazhtlZOgDBGGUGAYiKfiIuXS4AsLT1ZCufEDp5rw1ya6IeyXig_CR8PE8zw6fPmO35IPwcS_5B2asf2Jb8eEjvKqKDuGMHggfo1DtG9_OuZToc3kPr27FLTXF-v2MKcWqeyLpsrmY3gfwf9oOy38DAAD___X0gzM) is being developed in coordination with a regional working groups, a steering committee, industry groups, and international representatives. It's expected to be finalized this fall.

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18] | | | | | | Every major tech platform started the same way. ---

I've written before about [inefficient](https://substack.com/redirect/a26317f3-ef47-4150-b1a7-9f0fbc0d6206?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [government](https://substack.com/redirect/d9cef299-6429-4882-987e-249ab69328c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [spending](https://substack.com/redirect/4f89b16f-72fb-48b1-a08c-4db003900813?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), but for all of its issues, the government has played a huge role in decades-long declines in poverty, hunger, and childhood mortality.
Yes, it's imperfect, but the government has a mandate to take care of society's neediest. In spite of what DOGE would have to say, the goal of government isn't profitability; the goal is to make people's lives better.
Against that framing, Social Security has been an enormous success. When it began 90 years ago, seniors1 often faced homelessness and struggled to make ends meet.
America is much different today. Between healthcare and retirement, getting older remains expensive, but on the whole, seniors are much wealthier than they've ever been. Meanwhile, younger people are falling behind, less able to afford retirement, and less able to afford housing.
**The paradigm of American need has changed**. The federal government hasn't caught up.
[Subscribed](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9iZW5zYW11ZWxzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MTkzMzU1Mzk5LCJzIjoyNDQwMzk4LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1Ijo5MDUwMTE5MiwiaWF0IjoxNzc1NjUzMDM5LCJleHAiOjIwOTEyMjkwMzksImlzcyI6InB1Yi0wIiwic3ViIjoibGluay1yZWRpcmVjdCJ9._4kWQ44lF2OPAP-4ay6jLjBusBA2F0An494_2cf1s68?)
> _**Article summary:**_
> * _Social Security was, and is, an essential program. It 's also true that seniors have become substantially wealthier relative to the population since it was introduced._
> * _Meanwhile, younger and middle-aged Americans control much less wealth relative to their share of the U.S. population than was the case even a decade or two ago._
> * _Younger people in this country are increasingly unhappy, and we aren 't doing enough to help them._
>

### Social Security is an enormously successful program
Before talking about the needs of this country's under-65 cohort, we should first mention:
1. Taking care of the elderly is a societal mandate and something that a prosperous country _should_ be doing.
2. [Social Security is the most expensive federal program](https://substack.com/redirect/aae915ec-5af4-4b14-8980-d2756adfb4cd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), by a lot. Set aside any issues that Social Security has, if its goal was to make sure seniors were taken care of after retirement age, it's been wildly successful.
3. It's also overwhelmingly popular: [79% of Americans](https://substack.com/redirect/73e37333-8add-4068-9d87-547ffad095e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) say that Social Security benefits "should not be reduced in any way,"2 which is another part of the reason it's so difficult to reform.

When Social Security was [first introduced in 1935](https://substack.com/redirect/223d91d7-ea98-40d0-b3a3-33e982888159?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), it served a pressing societal need:
* [58% of people 65+ were living in poverty](https://substack.com/redirect/5c0a52d6-8def-422b-b57e-9f99c2520894?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), vs. 41% of adults ages 18-64.
* [About half of people 65+ were dependent](https://substack.com/redirect/4636c465-127b-4164-9799-bdffe4cdb172?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), generally on children and other family but sometimes on charity.
* It's tough to do an apples-to-apples comparison on homelessness, since it was understood and measured so differently 90 years ago than today. What is clear is that homelessness (as we'd now define it) was a _much_ larger problem for seniors, who were often forced to live in [almshouses](https://substack.com/redirect/2bc80c19-0bed-4d6c-b1a5-cf0dd6507f53?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) or other homes for the needy. Today, of the [61.2 million people 65+](https://substack.com/redirect/a973f082-15a0-4102-b9d2-077ab1fd511f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in the U.S., only [about 42,000](https://substack.com/redirect/4cb68906-089b-48eb-9487-e7fc32aad95f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--well under 0.1%--are homeless. There's always more work to do, but that's a triumph.

The rest of this article will be spent focusing on under-investment in people who _aren 't_ seniors. But it's important to recognize that Social Security is an enormous historical success and, for all of its costs, still essential for seniors today--[60% of seniors rely on the program for at least half of their income](https://substack.com/redirect/56cda6a9-0779-42d3-9757-f57136b78988?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
### Retirees reap far more benefits from federal money than young people
This article from _The Washington Post_ drew my attention last week.3
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/fd4e091e-6144-4090-b73f-7185defc6489?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
We will always need to spend more on seniors, per capita, than on younger people. But it's worth noting that the wellbeing and fortunes of American seniors have dramatically improved, especially since Medicare was introduced in the 1960s.
Since then, Social Security and Medicare4 have become two of the largest federal expenses. Here's what they look like against the overall federal budget:
* In 1970, seniors were 10% of the country's population, and Social Security and Medicare [made up 18.2% of the federal budget](https://substack.com/redirect/42f8e09c-2f28-4f42-87ea-7858b5cd209d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). That's **1.87 × their share of the U.S. population**.
* The percentage of Americans who are 65+ is at an all-time high, but [it's still only 18%](https://substack.com/redirect/effe57f7-377d-45ce-bccc-c5cc980490d4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Social Security and Medicare [made up 36.5% of the federal budget](https://substack.com/redirect/3b259c59-d644-4feb-ad62-577c1c620c73?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) last year. That's **2.04 × their share of the U.S. population**.

Spending on seniors has gone up relative to their share of the U.S. population, and these modest changes add up fast when the [combined budget](https://substack.com/redirect/3b259c59-d644-4feb-ad62-577c1c620c73?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of Social Security and Medicare is $2.5 trillion.5
What has changed much more dramatically: the wealth and welfare of seniors in this country vs. its younger people.
**Younger people have less wealth and own less housing than at any time in recent American history**. We're spending relatively more money on seniors even as they've gotten substantially wealthier.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=193355399&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MTkzMzU1Mzk5LCJpYXQiOjE3NzU2NTMwMzksImV4cCI6MTc3ODI0NTAzOSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.fMJGHuPvarxtWLWsG1ByaDHAF4IbrHqWA9T7YQeSkyI)
### Older people are becoming relatively wealthier, and younger people are falling behind
People over 70 hold [32% of the nation's net worth](https://substack.com/redirect/a6660cfd-1575-47bd-9e0b-027575b237c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). Even when you control for their growing share of the population, this is far more than over-70s held in 1989.
Meanwhile, the share for younger people is shrinking.6 18-to-54 year olds have fallen slightly as a percentage of the American population, but their share of the wealth has fallen dramatically:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/89a7f184-89f5-4755-bf75-c4f443741578?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
This divide is even more stark when it comes to homeownership. This year, for the first time, Americans who are 70+ years old hold more real estate wealth than people 40-54 years old.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/a84509b0-a11a-49d7-b641-efeb5dae3c32?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: [Redfin](https://substack.com/redirect/a84509b0-a11a-49d7-b641-efeb5dae3c32?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), Federal Reserve Board
That is a _dramatic_ change in who owns homes in the U.S. and an enormous decline in homeownership for middle-aged Americans, especially when you consider that homeownership is an extremely common path to building wealth in this country.7
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/c7b3c37e-7aa2-4cdd-b5f5-8f3f72fea3b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Middle-aged people's share of real estate wealth has dramatically fallen, whereas older people's wealth has dramatically grown. The [National Bureau of Economic Research captures this best](https://substack.com/redirect/065233ec-f808-41dd-85fc-b28b28b25567?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). (Emphasis added.)
> **In 1983, the average wealth of American households headed by someone aged 75 or older was 5 percent greater than the national average; in 2022, it was 55 percent greater.** Gains in owner-occupied housing and the stock market, and reduced mortgage debt, were key contributors.
To be clear, rising wealth among older people is not inherently a bad thing! Wealth creation is not zero-sum, and _[everyone](https://substack.com/redirect/f507c824-e107-4520-91cd-69ed15573149?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[ has gotten wealthier](https://substack.com/redirect/f507c824-e107-4520-91cd-69ed15573149?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) over the past few decades.
What's clear is that although seniors are no longer the most vulnerable in society, they still reap disproportionate benefits from federal spending. It's worth understanding the political drivers behind that.
### Seniors disproportionately decide elections
Part of the issue here is that young people don't vote. To state the obvious: elected officials are in the business of winning elections. And so they're going to craft policies that are appealing to their voters--who are, disproportionately, seniors.
After an uptick from 2016 to 2020, turnout among voters under 45 dropped precipitously in 2024. Meanwhile, the voting rate went _up_ for people 65+ between 2020 and 2024.8
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/4749658f-0e18-4eec-a4b2-418b19cdb0d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Even this doesn't tell the full story. Because of gerrymandering, 92% of U.S. House races are [functionally decided in primary elections](https://substack.com/redirect/3afff995-9369-428f-8117-885b7e198374?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).9 And voters in primaries are even older than voters in general elections: the [median age of a primary voter is 59](https://substack.com/redirect/f45c3b20-d982-4af8-90e5-95e6c3cf37f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg); in general elections, it's 54.10
All of this creates a dynamic that gives elected officials a very strong incentive to cater to older voters. I worry that leaves younger Americans in the dust, especially in light of changing fortunes for the country's seniors.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=193355399&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MTkzMzU1Mzk5LCJpYXQiOjE3NzU2NTMwMzksImV4cCI6MTc3ODI0NTAzOSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.fMJGHuPvarxtWLWsG1ByaDHAF4IbrHqWA9T7YQeSkyI)
### America's changing paradigm of need
Despite Social Security's issues--[namely, solvency](https://substack.com/redirect/05c33211-dd49-4e5b-bb21-a6e21b9554d4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--it is an important program for seniors in this country.
It's also increasingly clear that seniors today are in a much stronger position than they've ever been. Adjusting for inflation, [Baby Boomers control 2.3× more wealth](https://substack.com/redirect/f903736d-22c4-470a-becc-0b1124958a0a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) than the Greatest Generation did at their age in the early '80s.
Younger people aren't keeping up, which has consequences for affordability, family planning,11 and quality of life. But as much as anything else, this stands out to me: "in North America happiness has fallen so sharply for the young that they are now less happy than the old," according to the [World Happiness Report](https://substack.com/redirect/3720f08e-b981-494d-a80e-717148f54e88?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).12
I'm not suggesting cuts to Social Security in favor of the young, and in any event, touching Social Security is the [ultimate third rail of American politics](https://substack.com/redirect/bcd41b43-fe88-4b2e-b105-1220bc496831?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), so it's not going anywhere.
Nonetheless, it's abundantly clear that **the paradigm of American need has changed, and the federal government isn 't doing enough to help young people.**
More to come in Part 2.

1
Unless otherwise specified, "seniors" in this article will refer to Americans who are 65 and older.
2
Notably, even [73% of Americans between 18-29](https://substack.com/redirect/73e37333-8add-4068-9d87-547ffad095e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) say that Social Security benefits shouldn't be reduced. It's a broadly popular program.
3
The chart in this _[Washington Post](https://substack.com/redirect/fd4e091e-6144-4090-b73f-7185defc6489?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[ article](https://substack.com/redirect/fd4e091e-6144-4090-b73f-7185defc6489?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) is a bit misleading, namely because education funding comes almost entirely from local and state governments. Regardless, what's clear is that younger adults receive far less federal money, by their share of the population, than seniors:
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8c39042f-245a-4f15-9cd8-52861a300991?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
(To be very precise: the [Census data that I found was 25-64](https://substack.com/redirect/b80621f6-c2d0-4206-85b1-6f26a586ec62?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), but the data from the article was 26-64. So it's _very_ slightly off but not in a material way.)
4
There are some limited circumstances where Social Security and Medicare benefits don't go to seniors. If you have Lou Gehrig's Disease, for instance, [you're Medicare eligible even if you're under 65](https://substack.com/redirect/b48c8c84-ce3a-4d8b-a04e-daaff8a98a05?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
But these situations are pretty rare, and they don't materially change the numbers.
5
Large numbers are hard to conceptualize, but $2.5 trillion is $2,500,000,000,000. A 1% change is $25 billion ($25,000,000,000). We're talking about a lot of money!
6
A couple of sources here and then a note:
* [1987 demographic data](https://substack.com/redirect/11d8e075-4e1c-48e4-9470-4db123e8d824?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from the Census Bureau.
* [2024 demographic data](https://substack.com/redirect/b80621f6-c2d0-4206-85b1-6f26a586ec62?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from the Census Bureau.
* [Wealth data by generation and by year](https://substack.com/redirect/a6660cfd-1575-47bd-9e0b-027575b237c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

As with Footnote #3, the years didn't line up exactly. I used 1987 population data but 1989 wealth data, and I used 2024 population data but 2025 wealth data.
It won't materially impact the numbers, but I was constrained by what I could find from the Census Bureau, so I wanted to call out that the "year" in the table I'm footnoting is slightly off when it comes to the population data.
7
Sources:
* [1990 demographic data](https://substack.com/redirect/dc581cab-2744-4fb7-8438-54fd357d0583?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from the Census Bureau.
* [2024 demographic data](https://substack.com/redirect/b80621f6-c2d0-4206-85b1-6f26a586ec62?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from the Census Bureau.
* [Homeownership wealth data](https://substack.com/redirect/a84509b0-a11a-49d7-b641-efeb5dae3c32?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).

To make it a totally even comparison, I'm looking at 2024 Q4 in the homeownership wealth data, not the most recent 2025 data.
8
Even in a very large youth turnout year, 23% more people 65+ turned out to vote than people under 25. That [gap ballooned to 27% in 2024](https://substack.com/redirect/4749658f-0e18-4eec-a4b2-418b19cdb0d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
9
[Cook Political Report](https://substack.com/redirect/43527a30-1497-414f-895a-71fc1d895d43?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) says that 36 out of 435 seats are competitive, defined as "Lean D," "Toss Up," or "Lean R." That's 8%; the remainder, 92%, aren't competitive in general elections and are therefore functionally decided in primaries.
This is a [slightly different stat than I've shared before](https://substack.com/redirect/1053cdf3-e278-40ec-b0b8-0cc346d0df0a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), when I've said that 91% of U.S. House races are decided in primaries. What's changed? Well, voters aren't monoliths, and districts that weren't competitive can become competitive, and vice versa. But mostly, what changed was aggressive gerrymandering across the country.
This could become even more extreme if states like Florida and Virginia succeed in their efforts to gerrymander their states' Congressional districts.
10
For context, the median eligible voter is just 48 years old, more than a full decade younger than the people who are voting in primaries and deciding the vast majority of this country's U.S. House elections.
11
If people are having fewer kids, this has all sorts of long-term ramifications for the country, its workforce, and most of all, Social Security.
12
The concept of measuring happiness is squishy, but [the report](https://substack.com/redirect/3720f08e-b981-494d-a80e-717148f54e88?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) is put together by (among others) Gallup and the University of Oxford. So you can disagree with the methodology and inputs, but it's an academically rigorous report.
According to their data: for people 30 and under, America is the 62nd-happiest country. For people 60 and older, America is the 10th-happiest country. That's a huge difference! In aggregate, America is the 23rd-happiest country across all ages, but the older the cohort you're looking at, the happier we get.

It's also overwhelmingly popular: say that Social Security benefits "should not be reduced in any way,"2 which is another part of the reason it's so difficult to reform. Retirees reap far more benefits from federal money than young people This article from The Washington Post drew my attention last week.3 | | ---|---|--- We will always need to spend more on seniors, per capita, than on younger people. But it's worth noting that the wellbeing and fortunes of American seniors have dramatically improved, especially since Medicare was introduced in the 1960s. Since then, Social Security and Medicare4 have become two of the largest federal expenses. Here's what they look like against the overall federal budget: In 1970, seniors were 10% of the country's population, and Social Security and Medicare . That's 1.87 × their share of the U.S. population. The percentage of Americans who are 65+ is at an all-time high, but . Social Security and Medicare last year. That's 2.04 × their share of the U.S. population. Spending on seniors has gone up relative to their share of the U.S. population, and these modest changes add up fast when the of Social Security and Medicare is $2.5 trillion.5 What has changed much more dramatically: the wealth and welfare of seniors in this country vs. its younger people. Younger people have less wealth and own less housing than at any time in recent American history. We're spending relatively more money on seniors even as they've gotten substantially wealthier. Older people are becoming relatively wealthier, and younger people are falling behind People over 70 hold . Even when you control for their growing share of the population, this is far more than over-70s held in 1989. Meanwhile, the share for younger people is shrinking.6 18-to-54 year olds have fallen slightly as a percentage of the American population, but their share of the wealth has fallen dramatically: | | ---|---|--- This divide is even more stark when it comes to homeownership. This year, for the first time, Americans who are 70+ years old hold more real estate wealth than people 40-54 years old. | | ---|---|--- Source: , Federal Reserve Board That is a dramatic change in who owns homes in the U.S. and an enormous decline in homeownership for middle-aged Americans, especially when you consider that homeownership is an extremely common path to building wealth in this country.7 | | ---|---|--- Middle-aged people's share of real estate wealth has dramatically fallen, whereas older people's wealth has dramatically grown. The . (Emphasis added.) In 1983, the average wealth of American households headed by someone aged 75 or older was 5 percent greater than the national average; in 2022, it was 55 percent greater. Gains in owner-occupied housing and the stock market, and reduced mortgage debt, were key contributors. To be clear, rising wealth among older people is not inherently a bad thing! Wealth creation is not zero-sum, and over the past few decades. What's clear is that although seniors are no longer the most vulnerable in society, they still reap disproportionate benefits from federal spending. It's worth understanding the political drivers behind that. Seniors disproportionately decide elections Part of the issue here is that young people don't vote. To state the obvious: elected officials are in the business of winning elections. And so they're going to craft policies that are appealing to their voters--who are, disproportionately, seniors. After an uptick from 2016 to 2020, turnout among voters under 45 dropped precipitously in 2024. Meanwhile, the voting rate went up for people 65+ between 2020 and 2024.8 | | ---|---|--- Even this doesn't tell the full story. Because of gerrymandering, 92% of U.S. House races are And voters in primaries are even older than voters in general elections: the ; in general elections, it's 54.10 All of this creates a dynamic that gives elected officials a very strong incentive to cater to older voters. I worry that leaves younger Americans in the dust, especially in light of changing fortunes for the country's seniors. America's changing paradigm of need Despite Social Security's issues-- is an important program for seniors in this country. It's also increasingly clear that seniors today are in a much stronger position than they've ever been. Adjusting for inflation, than the Greatest Generation did at their age in the early '80s. Younger people aren't keeping up, which has consequences for affordability, family planning,11 and quality of life. But as much as anything else, this stands out to me: "in North America happiness has fallen so sharply for the young that they are now less happy than the old," according to the I'm not suggesting cuts to Social Security in favor of the young, and in any event, touching Social Security is the , so it's not going anywhere. Nonetheless, it's abundantly clear that the paradigm of American need has changed, and the federal government isn 't doing enough to help young people. More to come in Part 2. ? The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Williamson County, TN has had a county mayor for a generation. Mayor Anders has done an excellent job and I want to acknowledge how he was there at a time of explosive growth in Williamson County, making it the desired location from most of you in this room not born here. To amplify just how unique and special Wilco is let me tell you some facts:
In the rest of America, Counties don't have mayors. Counties will be typically headed by a board of some name. If they have an executive they will not be called a mayor. While the specific title "county mayor" is rare, Tennessee is one of the few states that formally uses the title for all its county executives. However, a similar executive role (county executive, county judge-executive, or county chair) exists in roughly 30 states, while others use a board of commissioners or supervisors.
Again, we've only known a mayor for 24 years and one of these two candidates will get to take over where he left off.
On that note, in Mayor Anders time in office right up to February of this year we got our 17th consecutive AAA bond rating on our debt, As of mid-2025, approximately 13 to 14 U.S. states hold a AAA rating--the highest possible credit rating--from all three major rating agencies (Moody's, S&P, and Fitch). Approximately 130 to 150 counties (roughly 2% of the ~3,100 U.S. counties) hold a AAA rating for their General Obligation (GO) bonds, which is the highest possible rating from major agencies such as Fitch Ratings, Moody's Investor Services, and S&P Global. And we are one of them. Something to be proud of.
How will we keep it, even NYC is on negative watch will make their cost of funds go up.
Williamson County Schools (WCS) is consistently ranked as the top school district in Tennessee, boasting high academic achievement with a 2024 district ACT composite of 25.2. The district is rated A+ for academics, teachers, and college prep, with high schools like Brentwood, Ravenwood, and Franklin ranked among the best in the state. With High Schools like Brentwood, Ravenwood & Franklin HS over 97% graduation rate.
How will we keep it with new arrivals every day and a teacher unaffordability crisis in the housing?
When Mayor Anders arrived, according to the 2000 U.S. Census, 126,638 people lived in Williamson County, Tennessee. This population figure marked a 56.3% increase from 1990, representing a significant growth period for the county at the turn of the millennium. Today approximately 272,061. The county has experienced rapid growth, adding over 24,000 residents since the 2020 census, driven by new developments and high demand in the Nashville suburban area. He welcomed 100%+ new arrivals during his tenure.
How will we steward this growth with land, debt and infrastructure including traffic already a daily concern?
Let's find out what our possible next county mayor has planned for us? Please don't let this be a low turn out vote, some anticipate 10% or less. The stakes are high as I explained. I'm encouraged by y'all's willingness to come out on a Monday Night and her from these two excellent candidates. Please enjoy the forum and thank you for being active citizens in the best county in the best country on Earth...and God bless America.

| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
Friends,
To those celebrating, I want to wish you and your loved ones a meaningful and joyful Passover.
As we enter the final days of the holiday, we reflect on the crossing of the Red Sea, a powerful moment of courage, faith, and liberation. It's a reminder that, even in the face of overwhelming obstacles, change is possible and freedom is worth fighting for.
As we carry that story with us into these last days, we're also called to see the struggles that continue today, both around the world and here at home, and to hold onto the responsibility to build a more just and compassionate future.
Wishing you a beautiful end to your Passover, filled with reflection, connection, and hope.
Chag Sameach,Yen Bailey

| | | Yen Bailey’s journey began with her parents, who fled war-torn Vietnam. Her father, a South Vietnamese Air Force pilot, bravely escaped the fall of Saigon by flying with his crew and dozens of Vietnamese refugees. They settled in Destin, Florida, where Yen and her brother were born and raised. Witnessing her parents' sacrifices and resilience deeply influenced Yen, inspiring her to pursue a career in law and public service.

[ ](https://yenbaileyforcongress.us9.list-manage.com/track/click?u=642870bb478010796c7288d8f&id=fda6edce68&e=58216231a8)

A Tallahassee-based attorney and Tulane University and Florida State University Law School graduate, Yen has dedicated her career to public service. She served as a Senior Attorney for the Guardian ad Litem Program and spent over 13 years as an ethics attorney at The Florida Bar. Committed to her family, Yen stepped away from her law career at the Bar to care for her elderly father.

Yen is a proud wife and mother. She cherishes time with her husband, Steve Bailey, a lawyer and professor at Florida State University and former Army Green Beret, and their two teenage sons.

Yen’s dedication to civic engagement led her to co-found Every Vote Florida, a nonprofit voter outreach organization, where she served as Vice President. She also served on the board of Friends of the LeRoy Collins Public Library System, promoting literacy and supporting public libraries in Leon County.

Yen is running for office to address the needs and challenges of the average Floridian in the panhandle, believing her opponent, Neal Dunn, has failed to do so. For years, many in the district have felt neglected and left behind by Dunn, and Yen wants to be a voice for all in Washington D.C.

With her extensive background in public service and dedication to the community, Yen Bailey offers a fresh perspective for District 2. Her journey from the daughter of immigrants to a congressional candidate embodies the American dream and the power of perseverance.

---
